scenes.visual: Title card: Multiply, Don't Add.

scenes.tts: Your cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's. So why is its surface roughly a thousand times larger?
scenes.visual: A mouse cortex and a human cortex drawn as flat, unfolded sheets. Labels: thickness about 2 times; area about 1,000 times. Question on screen.
scenes.narration: Your cortex is only about twice as thick as a mouse's. So why is its surface roughly a thousand times larger?

scenes.tts: Almost all of the gain is sideways. How does a brain build more of the same wall?
scenes.visual: The size factor split on screen: height times 2, area times about 1,000. An arrow pointing sideways.
scenes.narration: Almost all of the gain is sideways. How does a brain build more of the same wall?

scenes.tts: Compare two kinds of division.
scenes.visual: A single progenitor cell at the bottom edge of the sheet, by the ventricle.
scenes.narration: Compare two kinds of division.

scenes.tts: In a symmetric proliferative division, one progenitor makes two. If every progenitor does this once, the pool doubles.
scenes.visual: One cell splits into two progenitors. Label: one division, plus 1 progenitor. Then a row of four cells all split at once. Label: a full round, pool times 2.
scenes.narration: In a symmetric proliferative division, one progenitor makes two. If every progenitor does this once, the pool doubles.

scenes.tts: In an asymmetric neurogenic division, it makes one progenitor and one neuron. The pool stays the same size.
scenes.visual: One cell splits into a progenitor and a neuron. Label: asymmetric neurogenic. Pool counter fixed; neuron counter ticks up by one.
scenes.narration: In an asymmetric neurogenic division, it makes one progenitor and one neuron. The pool stays the same size.

scenes.tts: The radial glia lining the ventricle, the founders, divide symmetrically first. Later they switch to making neurons.
scenes.visual: A row of founder cells along the ventricle doubles, then switches to making neurons.
scenes.narration: The radial glia lining the ventricle, the founders, divide symmetrically first. Later they switch to making neurons.

scenes.tts: Pasko Rakic showed that young neurons climb radial glial fibres. He argued that they stack into columns.
scenes.visual: Name card: Pasko Rakic, fetal rhesus monkey. Neurons climb one fibre and stack above the patch where they were born, the youngest on top.
scenes.narration: Pasko Rakic showed that young neurons climb radial glial fibres. He argued that they stack into columns.

scenes.tts: In nineteen eighty-eight, he proposed the radial unit hypothesis. If every unit takes up about the same patch of surface, the number of units sets the area. The neurons per unit set the thickness.
scenes.caption: In 1988, he proposed the radial unit hypothesis. If every unit takes up about the same patch of surface, the number of units sets the area. The neurons per unit set the thickness.
scenes.visual: Title: the radial unit hypothesis, 1988. Columns side by side; across the row, number of units, area (same patch per unit); up one column, neurons per unit, thickness.
scenes.narration: In 1988, he proposed the radial unit hypothesis. If every unit takes up about the same patch of surface, the number of units sets the area. The neurons per unit set the thickness.

scenes.tts: Predict. Species B gets three extra rounds of symmetric division, before the switch. Species C gets three extra asymmetric divisions per unit, after it, each adding one neuron.
scenes.visual: On screen: A, each unit makes about 100 neurons. B, three extra symmetric rounds. C, three extra asymmetric divisions per unit.
scenes.narration: Predict. Species B gets three extra rounds of symmetric division, before the switch. Species C gets three extra asymmetric divisions per unit, after it, each adding one neuron.

scenes.tts: Which species gains more neurons? And which one gains area?
scenes.visual: Question card over the three species.
scenes.narration: Which species gains more neurons? And which one gains area?

scenes.visual: Question card held, with the A, B and C setup still on screen.

scenes.tts: Species B. Doubling three times gives eight times the units, so, with the same patch per unit, eight times the area.
scenes.visual: On screen: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. Species B's sheet grows to eight times the area; columns stay the same height.
scenes.narration: Species B. Doubling three times gives eight times the units, so, with the same patch per unit, eight times the area.

scenes.tts: Species C gains about three percent more neurons, and no extra units, so no extra area.
scenes.visual: On screen: 103 instead of 100, about 3 percent more. Species C's columns grow very slightly taller; area unchanged.
scenes.narration: Species C gains about three percent more neurons, and no extra units, so no extra area.

scenes.visual: Both results side by side.

scenes.tts: Doubling multiplies. Adding only adds.
scenes.visual: Caption: doubling multiplies; adding only adds.
scenes.narration: Doubling multiplies. Adding only adds.

scenes.tts: Back to the mouse. Ten doublings make about a thousandfold. So, in this model, with every unit the same size, ten extra rounds would close the gap.
scenes.visual: On screen: 2 to the power 10 = 1,024. The mouse sheet doubles ten times to reach the human sheet.
scenes.narration: Back to the mouse. Ten doublings make about a thousandfold. So, in this model, with every unit the same size, ten extra rounds would close the gap.

scenes.tts: Our brain is about three times a chimpanzee's. If our cortical area differs by a similar factor, the gap is under two rounds.
scenes.visual: On screen: about 3 times, between 2 to the 1 and 2 to the 2. Label: if cortical area differs by a similar factor.
scenes.narration: Our brain is about three times a chimpanzee's. If our cortical area differs by a similar factor, the gap is under two rounds.

scenes.tts: Rakic made a related argument for primates in nineteen ninety-five. A delay of a few cell cycles before the switch could greatly enlarge the cortex.
scenes.caption: Rakic made a related argument for primates in 1995. A delay of a few cell cycles before the switch could greatly enlarge the cortex.
scenes.visual: Name card: Rakic, 1995. A founder pool delayed by a few cycles before switching.
scenes.narration: Rakic made a related argument for primates in 1995. A delay of a few cell cycles before the switch could greatly enlarge the cortex.

scenes.tts: In mice, a stabilized form of beta-catenin kept more progenitors dividing. The cortex grew in area, and buckled into folds.
scenes.caption: In mice, a stabilized form of β-catenin kept more progenitors dividing. The cortex grew in area, and buckled into folds.
scenes.visual: Name card: Chenn and Walsh, 2002. A smooth mouse cortex enlarges and buckles into folds, from a larger ventricular surface. Label: schematic.
scenes.narration: In mice, a stabilized form of β-catenin kept more progenitors dividing. The cortex grew in area, and buckled into folds.

scenes.tts: That shows extra founder divisions can enlarge the sheet, not how primates did it.
scenes.visual: Caption: can enlarge the sheet; not how primates did it.
scenes.narration: That shows extra founder divisions can enlarge the sheet, not how primates did it.

scenes.tts: In organoids, human cells took longer than ape cells to become radial glia. The human organoids grew larger. Neither test was done in a developing human brain.
scenes.visual: Three organoids labelled human, chimpanzee, gorilla. A timer runs longer on the human one; it grows larger.
scenes.narration: In organoids, human cells took longer than ape cells to become radial glia. The human organoids grew larger. Neither test was done in a developing human brain.

scenes.tts: Multiply, don't add. Extra rounds of doubling can multiply the neurons a cortex makes.
scenes.visual: Guiding-idea card: Multiply, don't add. Extra doubling rounds can multiply neuron output.
scenes.narration: Multiply, don't add. Extra rounds of doubling can multiply the neurons a cortex makes.

scenes.tts: That is the leading explanation for our big cortex, and nearly all of the gain went into area.
scenes.visual: The card adds: leading explanation; the gain went into area. Small print: tested in animals and organoids, not a developing human brain.
scenes.narration: That is the leading explanation for our big cortex, and nearly all of the gain went into area.

scenes.tts: So for every cell and gene that follows, ask what it changes.
scenes.visual: Closing card: what does it change? More doubling, more time, or something else?
scenes.narration: So for every cell and gene that follows, ask what it changes.

scenes.visual: Closing card held.
